Solace
SOL-as
v. (to comfort; to take delight or consolation in)
Hebrew alas, to rejoice or take delight. Latin solari, to console, giving solatium, comfort. The word is honourable in itself, which is precisely what makes its one biblical occurrence so disturbing.

Biblical Definition

Come, let us take our fill of love until the morning: let us solace ourselves with loves. This is the speech of the strange woman in Proverbs 7, and the father who records it for his son has chosen to quote her at length rather than merely to warn against her. That is deliberate instruction. The sentence uses the vocabulary of comfort and delight — solace, love — because temptation never presents itself in the language of what it actually is. She speaks of comfort; the chapter has already told us that her house is the way to hell, going down to the chambers of death. The father also tells the son exactly what does the work, and it is not beauty but speech: with her much fair speech she caused him to yield, with the flattering of her lips she forced him. Her mouth is the instrument, as it is at Proverbs 5:3 — the lips of a strange woman drop as an honeycomb, and her mouth is smoother than oil. And the sinner's own precaution is quoted too, in the line about her husband: he is not at home, he is gone a long journey. The whole seduction is built on a calculation about who is watching. Scripture's answer throughout is that the calculation is wrong, since the ways of man are before the eyes of the LORD, and he pondereth all his goings.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): to comfort; to console; to cheer; to amuse; to allay grief or trouble.

expand to see more

SOLACE, v.t. To cheer in grief or under calamity; to comfort; to relieve in affliction; to console.

SOLACE, v.t. To allay; to assuage; as, to solace grief.

SOLACE, n. Comfort in grief; alleviation of grief or anxiety; that which relieves in distress.

FLATTERY, n. False praise; commendation bestowed for the purpose of gaining favor and influence.

SEDUCE, v.t. To draw aside or entice from the path of rectitude and duty; to corrupt; to lead astray.

Key Scripture

Proverbs 7:18 — "Come, let us take our fill of love until the morning: let us solace ourselves with loves."

Proverbs 7:21 — "With her much fair speech she caused him to yield, with the flattering of her lips she forced him."

Proverbs 7:27 — "Her house is the way to hell, going down to the chambers of death."

Proverbs 5:3 — "For the lips of a strange woman drop as an honeycomb, and her mouth is smoother than oil:"

Modern Corruption

Sexual sin is reframed as the pursuit of intimacy and comfort, which is exactly the vocabulary the tempter uses in this chapter; Proverbs quotes the pitch and then names the destination.

expand to see more

The strange woman does not say come and commit adultery. She speaks of love, of filling, of solace, and the chapter preserves her words so that a young man will recognise the register when he hears it. The contemporary version is identical in substance: the affair described as a connection, the pornography as a relief from stress, the departure from a covenant as honesty about one's needs. Every one of these is the language of comfort attached to the thing Scripture calls a way to the chambers of death. The dictionary notes that the corruption here is not new and has never needed updating, because it was fully developed when Solomon wrote.

The second observation concerns the instrument, and it cuts against the assumption that lust is chiefly visual. Proverbs says twice that the seduction is verbal — with her much fair speech she caused him to yield, and her mouth is smoother than oil. What ensnares the young man is being spoken to in a way he wants to be spoken to. That is why Scripture's counsel is not merely to look away but to guard the ear and the company, and why the chapter's positive remedy is that the father's own words be bound upon the fingers and written upon the table of the heart. One speech is answered by another.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew alas (H5965), to rejoice or delight; ravah (H7301), to drink one's fill; zarah (H2114), strange or foreign; chalaq (H2505), smooth or flattering.

expand to see more

Hebrew alas (H5965) — to delight, to take pleasure; rendered solace, its only such rendering.

Hebrew ravah (H7301) — to be saturated, to take one's fill; rendered take our fill.

Hebrew zarah (H2114) — to be strange, foreign; the strange woman of Proverbs.

Hebrew chelqah (H2513) — smoothness, flattery; behind the flattering of her lips.

Hebrew sheol (H7585) — the grave, hell; where the chapter says her house leads.

Usage

"“let us solace ourselves with loves” — sin speaking the language of comfort."

"“with her much fair speech she caused him to yield” — the instrument named."

"“her house is the way to hell” — the destination the pitch omits."
